title: Virtues for your state (III.1)
hookLine: the calm one in the group chat, the fixer at work, the kid at home: does each role need a different kind of good?
carry: fit the virtue to the life
tomorrow: the line won't move and you're already late. now what?

lines: THE CALM ONE. THE FIXER. THE KID.
cards: In the group chat you're the calm one. At work you're the fixer. At home you're still the one who gets reminded about the trash.
Same person, three jobs. Does each of them need a different kind of good? Francis de Sales says yes, mostly.
Part three of his book turns from prayer to daily living, and its first move is to fit the virtue to the person.

teach.b: So, the question: is goodness one size for everyone? Francis's answer comes as a rule. Practice above all the virtues your own state of life and its duties ask of you.

teach.h: A BISHOP'S, A SOLDIER'S, A WIDOW'S.
teach.b: A bishop's virtues aren't a prince's, he says, and a soldier's aren't those of a married woman or a widow. But some virtues belong in every life, and he names patience, gentleness and humility among them. Then a warning.
People are drawn to the virtues that look impressive, and pass over the plain ones their days actually need.
He asks for the reverse: useful before showy. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that it is better to do your own duty, even imperfectly, than another person's duty well.

teach.h: FIT THE VIRTUE TO THE LIFE.
teach.b: The shared ground: goodness is lived in the life you've actually been given, not in a borrowed one. And one honest difference.
Krishna is speaking of dharma, the duty that comes with one's place in life, and he says it to a warrior on the edge of a battle.
Francis is speaking of virtues, habits of the heart grown inside a Christian life, and he keeps some of them, like patience, for everyone. Two traditions, each in its own words.

how: Some Catholics choose one virtue to work on for a season, often one their family, work or calling especially needs, and bring it to prayer and to confession.

games.q: what does “virtues for your state” mean?
o: the virtues a country asks of its citizens
good habits that only clergy and religious can keep
the virtues your own role and duties ask of you

games.q: virtues for your state — tap the pairs.
p: your station and calling in life
what your days need, not what wins notice
better your own duty, done imperfectly

s: for Francis, virtue is one standard, practiced the same way by everyone
he says to practice first the virtues your own state and duties ask of you.
he names patience, gentleness and humility among virtues every life needs
the rule sets an order of work; it doesn't split people into camps.
Francis and the Gita are saying exactly the same thing
neighbors: both fit goodness to your own life, but Krishna speaks of dharma to a warrior, Francis of virtues in a Christian life.

games.q: a nurse you know spends every day off volunteering for three causes and comes to her shifts and her kids exhausted. by Francis's rule, what comes first?
o: the virtues her nursing and her family ask of her.
the volunteering, since it's the more generous work.
whatever looks holiest to the people around her.
games.why: Francis puts the virtues of your own state and duties first, and warns against preferring the impressive ones to the useful.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write the roles your days are made of: student, worker, parent, friend, neighbor. Circle one, and through the sit let the single virtue it needs most from you come to mind, then write that word beside it.
If you pray, you can ask God for that one.

wordCard.voice: Virtues for your state. Francis's counsel to practice first the virtues your own life and its duties ask for.

carryVoice: Your line: fit the virtue to the life, the one your days actually need, not the one that shows. Go gently.
